blindSummary:
This is one of the safest countries in the world for transgender visitors. A 2019 gender-autonomy law allows self-defined gender registration without diagnosis or surgery, non-binary people can use an "X" marker, and discrimination on grounds of gender identity and expression is banned in services and employment. General crime rates are very low.

Local travel businesses actively accommodate trans visitors: a dedicated traveller guide from the national LGBT tourism body reports that most swimming pools in the capital area offer private or gender-neutral changing rooms, that using binary changing rooms is legal and common, and that trans visitors generally are told they need not worry about their safety. Emergency services maintain dedicated guidance for queer victims of abuse and hate crime.

Residual risks are small: potential hate-crime reports have risen in recent years (from very low absolute levels), the country's hate-crime law works through sentencing aggravation rather than a standalone offence, and occasional misgendering — usually unintentional — still occurs.
blindOutOfScope: The country's principal hazards are natural (weather, road conditions, geothermal and volcanic areas) and affect all travellers equally.
blindSourceSummaries: National LGBT tourism-body travel information for trans and non-binary travellers (updated 2025): since 2019, informed-consent healthcare and name/gender change via the civil registry without medical diagnosis (under-18s with parental consent); social attitudes accepting; low crime; most capital-area swimming pools offer private, gender-neutral locker rooms usable without questions.

International LGBT-rights organisation country overview (updated March 2026): marriage and adoption; employment discrimination banned on SOGIESC grounds since 2018; self-determination gender markers and 'X' documents; intersex surgeries on minors banned in most cases; a conversion-practices ban with criminal penalties took effect January 2024; high public acceptance; Pride parades with several thousand attendees and government participation.

Crowd-sourced safety data: homosexuality legal, marriage legal, gender change with no restrictions, nonbinary recognised, hate-crime protections cover SOGI, discrimination illegal, full ban on intersex infant surgery, conversion therapy banned, bathroom access protected. First of 121 surveyed regions for 'good place' for gay and lesbian people (93%).

Regional security-organisation page on this country's hate-crime legislation: the general penal code lists gender characteristics, sexuality and gender identity among aggravating factors when deciding punishment.

Regional security-organisation page on the country's national hate-crime frameworks: data collected by the national police commissioner include discrimination and defamation cases; no systematic collection of hate-crime statistics.

National emergency-helpline information page on hate crime: the term 'hate crime' does not appear in statute, but victim status (including gender identity and sexual characteristics) must be considered in sentencing under a general penal-code provision; explains hate speech and discrimination definitions.

The same emergency-helpline page on abuse against queer people: queer people are more likely to be victims of violence; marginalisation, fear of isolation, and barriers to seeking help; all public services available to victims.

National news site (Aug 2025): potential hate crimes recorded by police have risen - 16 cases in 2023 (triple the prior year), 11 in 2024, 7 so far in 2025; the national queer organisation says cases linked to gender identity have become more common since 2018 and calls for stronger hate-crime legislation.
A foreign government's travel advice for this destination: safety and security. General travel advice, not trans-specific.

Official government page on the national equality complaints committee: individuals and NGOs can refer equality-act violations; the committee issues binding written rulings; advisors at the state equality directorate provide support.

Independent weekly (Aug 2019): feature on trans rights - the old process (six paid psychiatric interviews, a year of 'living as your gender' before HRT/surgery) is being replaced by the informed-consent model, which the country has more or less legally adopted - the trans person is the authority on their own gender.
blindLocalsOnly: The 2019 gender-autonomy law's self-defined registration and X marker are resident-facing processes.
